essay_levels.descriptor: Convincing, critical and exploratory. A sustained, well-structured argument; quotations chosen precisely and woven in; perceptive analysis of the writer's methods and their effects, with subject terminology used judiciously; context explored and linked convincingly to the writer's ideas.
Thoughtful and developed. A considered, coherent response; well-chosen references; examination of the writer's methods and effects with apt terminology; thoughtful links between context and the text.

Clear and explained. A clear response to task and text; effective use of references; clear explanation of the writer's methods and their effects with relevant terminology; clear understanding of context linked to the text.
Some explanation. Some explained response; references used to support points; some identification and explanation of methods; some awareness of context.
Supported and relevant comments. Relevant comments backed by some reference; awareness of the writer making choices; some awareness of context.
Simple, explicit comments. Simple comments with little reference to the text; little awareness of methods or context.

paragraph_levels.descriptor: Perceptive, detailed analysis of the writer's methods with precise references and apt terminology; ideas linked to the writer's purpose or context where relevant.
Clear explanation of how methods create meaning, with well-chosen references and relevant terminology.
Some explanation of meaning with some reference to the text; methods identified but only partly explained.
Simple comments about the character or idea, mostly retelling, with little or no analysis.

shared.spag: AO4 (4 marks), separate from the 30: 4 = consistently accurate spelling and punctuation and a wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures; 2-3 = considerable accuracy and a good range; 1 = reasonable accuracy and a reasonable range with errors that don't hinder meaning; 0 = errors hinder meaning or the answer is not relevant.

questions.subtopic: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth as characters
questions.question_text:
Read the following extract from Act 1 Scene 5 of Macbeth. Lady Macbeth has just read Macbeth's letter and learned that King Duncan will stay at their castle tonight.

The raven himself is hoarse
That croaks the fatal entrance of Duncan
Under my battlements. Come, you spirits
That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here,
And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full
Of direst cruelty! Make thick my blood;
Stop up the access and passage to remorse,
That no compunctious visitings of nature
Shake my fell purpose, nor keep peace between
The effect and it! Come to my woman's breasts,
And take my milk for gall, you murd'ring ministers,
Wherever in your sightless substances
You wait on nature's mischief!

Starting with this speech, explore how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a powerful woman.

Write about:
• how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth in this speech
• how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth in the play as a whole.

[30 marks + 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar]
indicative: Her invocation of spirits ('Come, you spirits') links her to the supernatural and to the witches
'Unsex me here': she rejects the expectations of femininity to gain the cruelty she thinks power needs
Imagery of blood, poison ('milk for gall') and darkness presents her ambition as unnatural
Imperatives and exclamations show her control and determination
Elsewhere she dominates Macbeth: questioning his masculinity in Act 1 Scene 7, planning the murder, taking charge after it
Her power fades: excluded from Macbeth's later plans, then the sleepwalking scene (Act 5 Scene 1) and her death
Jacobean context: the Great Chain of Being, beliefs about witchcraft and the supernatural (James I), expectations of women as obedient wives
Power that defies the natural order is shown to be destructive and short-lived

questions.topic: A Christmas Carol: Plot, Character & Context
questions.question_text:
Read the following extract from Stave 1 of A Christmas Carol, in which Scrooge is introduced.

Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster. The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shrivelled his cheek, stiffened his gait; made his eyes red, his thin lips blue; and spoke out shrewdly in his grating voice. A frosty rime was on his head, and on his eyebrows, and his wiry chin. He carried his own low temperature always about with him; he iced his office in the dog-days; and didn't thaw it one degree at Christmas.

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents Scrooge as an outsider in society.

Write about:
• how Dickens presents Scrooge in this extract
• how Dickens presents Scrooge as an outsider in the novel as a whole.

[30 marks]
indicative: The list of verbs ('squeezing, wrenching, grasping...') builds a picture of greed and isolation
Similes 'hard and sharp as flint' and 'solitary as an oyster' suggest he is closed off, though the oyster may hide a pearl, hinting at change
Cold imagery: he carries his 'own low temperature', so his coldness separates him from others
He rejects Fred's invitation and the charity collectors; people and even dogs avoid him
The Ghost of Christmas Past shows how he became isolated (lonely childhood, losing Belle)
By Stave 5 he is welcomed into family and society: the outsider is redeemed
Victorian context: the Poor Law and workhouses, Malthus ('decrease the surplus population'), Dickens's concern for social responsibility
Dickens uses Scrooge's isolation to criticise selfish attitudes to the poor

questions.topic: An Inspector Calls: Plot, Character & Context
questions.subtopic: The Inspector as a dramatic device
questions.question_text:
How does Priestley use the character of the Inspector to present his ideas about social responsibility in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
• what the Inspector says and does
• how Priestley uses the Inspector to present his ideas about social responsibility.

[30 marks + 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar]
indicative: The Inspector's interruption of Birling's speech about every man looking after himself
He controls the pace and structure of the play: one line of enquiry at a time, the photograph
His language is direct, blunt and morally charged; stage directions about 'massiveness, solidity and purposefulness'
The final speech: 'We are members of one body', 'fire and blood and anguish'
His name (Goole / ghoul) and mysterious status; possibly a supernatural or symbolic figure
He acts as Priestley's mouthpiece for socialist ideas
Contrast between the younger generation (Sheila, Eric) who learn and the older (Mr and Mrs Birling) who don't
Context: set in 1912, written in 1945; dramatic irony about the Titanic and war; post-war hope for a welfare state

questions.topic: Power and Conflict Poetry: Comparing Poems & Techniques
questions.question_text:
Ozymandias, by Percy Bysshe Shelley

I met a traveller from an antique land,
Who said—"Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert. . . . Near them, on the sand,
Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,
The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed;
And on the pedestal, these words appear:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away."

Compare how poets present the effects of power in 'Ozymandias' and in one other poem from 'Power and conflict'.

[30 marks]
indicative: Ozymandias: power is temporary; nature and time destroy human pride
The 'shattered visage' and 'sneer of cold command' show arrogance and cruelty
Irony of the inscription against 'Nothing beside remains'
Form: a sonnet with an irregular rhyme scheme, perhaps reflecting broken power; framed narrative distances the king
Good comparisons: My Last Duchess (controlling power of a man over a woman), London (power of institutions over people), Extract from The Prelude (power of nature), Storm on the Island
Comparison should cover ideas and methods (language, structure, form) for both poems
Context: Shelley's Romantic and revolutionary views, his hostility to tyranny
A strong answer compares throughout rather than writing about each poem separately

questions.question_text:
In Act 2 Scene 1, just before he murders Duncan, Macbeth says:

"Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee."

Analyse how Shakespeare uses this soliloquy to present Macbeth's state of mind. Write one or two developed paragraphs.

[8 marks]
indicative: The question shows confusion and doubt: he can't trust his own senses
The dagger may be a hallucination caused by guilt, or a supernatural temptation
'The handle toward my hand' suggests the murder is being offered to him; he is being drawn towards it
The imperative 'Come, let me clutch thee' shows a desperate, grasping ambition
A soliloquy lets the audience see his private fears, building tension before the murder
Links to the supernatural and to the witches' influence

questions.topic: A Christmas Carol: Language, Themes & Quotations
questions.question_text:
In Stave 3, the Ghost of Christmas Present reveals two children, Ignorance and Want, hidden under his robe.

Analyse how Dickens uses Ignorance and Want to present his ideas about poverty. Write one or two developed paragraphs.

[8 marks]
indicative: They are allegorical figures, not real children, representing society's neglect
Descriptions such as 'wretched, abject, frightful, hideous, miserable' shock the reader
The warning about the boy (Ignorance) and 'Doom' shows Dickens believed ignorance was most dangerous
The Ghost throws Scrooge's own words back at him ('Are there no prisons? Are there no workhouses?')
Context: Dickens's concern about child poverty, the ragged schools and the 1834 Poor Law
The scene is a turning point in Scrooge's understanding of his responsibility

questions.topic: An Inspector Calls: Language, Themes & Quotations
questions.question_text:
Explain how Priestley presents Sheila as changing during An Inspector Calls. Use references to the play. Write one or two developed paragraphs.

[8 marks]
indicative: At the start she is excited about her engagement and childish ('mummy'); stage directions describe her as 'very pleased with life'
She feels genuine guilt about Eva's dismissal from Milwards
She sees through Gerald and understands the Inspector's methods ('he's giving us the rope')
By the end she rejects her parents' attitudes and accepts responsibility
Priestley uses her to show the younger generation's capacity to change and hope for the future
Context: changing roles of women and Priestley's socialist message

questions.topic: Power and Conflict Poetry: Poem Knowledge & Context
questions.subtopic: The Charge of the Light Brigade and Exposure
questions.question_text:
Analyse how Wilfred Owen presents the suffering of soldiers in 'Exposure'. Write one or two developed paragraphs, using references to the poem.

[8 marks]
indicative: The weather is the real enemy: 'the merciless iced east winds that knive us'
The repeated refrain 'But nothing happens' shows boredom, waiting and futility
Half-rhymes and long, slow lines create unease and a sense of things not resolving
Present tense and collective 'we' make the suffering shared and immediate
Soldiers' minds drift home, but 'on us the doors are closed', showing despair
Context: Owen's own experience in the trenches in winter 1917; protest against the glorification of war
